title: Prayer and medicine
hook: Judaism values both doctors and prayer
tomorrow: Saba's home, and Mom hasn't slept. who takes care of the carer?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a verse that brings God into a seat on the bus: rise before the hoary head, because only your heart knows if you saw. Honor the old. Today, an old body needs fixing.
screen: `HONOR THE OLD.` → `AN OLD BODY NEEDS FIXING.`

segments.voice: Two screens open at once. One is a patient portal: surgery Tuesday, arrive at six, nothing to eat after midnight. The other is the family chat, where an aunt has written: praying for you!!! So which one is doing the healing? Inside Jewish tradition, two serious voices answer that question differently, and both quote the Bible.
screen: `A PATIENT PORTAL.` → `PRAYING FOR YOU!!!` → `WHICH ONE IS DOING THE HEALING?`

segments.voice: The first voice remembers King Asa. The book of Chronicles says that when he fell ill, "yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians." Nachmanides, the medieval commentator, wrote that in a time when people lived fully close to God, they wouldn't need doctors at all. Its best case: healing comes from God in the end, and a waiting room can make you forget that. The second voice starts in Exodus, in a law about an injury: the one who caused it must see that the injured person is thoroughly healed. The Talmud, in Bava Kamma, reads that line and says: from here, the doctor is given permission to heal. Maimonides was himself a physician. Later law codes go further and call healing a mitzvah, a commandment. Its best case: the body is a gift, and neglecting it is no kind of faith. Notice what the first voice is really worried about: Asa sought the doctors instead of God, not as well as. And Jewish practice, as it's lived, mostly holds both together. A patient sees the surgeon. The community says a prayer called the Mi Sheberakh, asking for a refuah shleimah, a complete healing, of body and of spirit. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud finds the doctor's permission to heal inside a law about a fistfight.
screen: `ASA: THE PHYSICIANS, NOT GOD.` · `BAVA KAMMA: PERMISSION TO HEAL.` · `INSTEAD OF, OR AS WELL AS?` · `THE SURGEON, AND A MI SHEBERAKH.` · then, large: `DOCTORS AND PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Name one health task you've been putting off: a checkup, a refill, a dentist, a walk your body keeps asking for. Then name what's in the way. Then choose one small first step, and when you'll take it.
screen: `ONE HEALTH TASK.` · `WHAT'S IN THE WAY.` · `ONE SMALL STEP, AND WHEN.`

segments.voice: Prayer and medicine: the surgeon's hands and the community's prayer, held together. The Talmud gives the doctor permission; the Mi Sheberakh asks for complete healing.
Pocket this one: doctors and prayer, as well as, not instead of. Wishing a refuah shleimah to anyone who needs one.

howItsDone: Jews seek medical care, which later codes of Jewish law call a mitzvah, and in synagogue a Mi Sheberakh prayer is often said for the sick by name, asking for a complete healing of body and spirit.

chat.says: saba's surgery is tuesday. he was a PHARMACIST and he asked shul to say a mi sheberakh. why both?
options: Both fit. The Talmud gives doctors permission to heal, and the community prays for healing too.
Mixed signals. Asking for prayers means he doesn't really trust the surgeons.

chat.meaning: Bava Kamma reads Exodus as permission for the doctor to heal; the Mi Sheberakh asks for complete healing. Jewish practice holds doctors and prayer together.

Nachmanides.meaning: a medieval Spanish rabbi and Torah commentator, also called Ramban

Bava Kamma.meaning: a tractate of the Talmud about damages and injuries

Maimonides.meaning: a medieval Jewish scholar, physician and author of a law code

Mi Sheberakh.meaning: a prayer said for the sick in synagogue

mitzvah.meaning: a commandment; also, a good deed

sources.quoted: yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians.
